title: 40 AI Suppliers. 9 Survivors. 1 I Bought.
subtitle: I screened the AI supply chain after the crash. Nine are still growing 50%+, making cash and holding more cash than debt. I bought one of them on Friday.

content.text: Full disclosure first:
on Friday I bought Credo ($CRDO) in my own account. It is not in the BBP Portfolio. Everything below is how I got there, including the parts that worry me.
The AI trade just had its worst stretch of the year.
The iShares Semiconductor ETF closed Tuesday 33% below its June high. The Nasdaq-100 is 11% below its October record.
When everything falls together, the market stops looking at the businesses. Good and bad companies get sold the same way.
So I asked a simple question: which AI suppliers are still doing great business, and got a lot cheaper anyway?
THE SCREEN

I took 40 companies that sell into AI data centers: chips, memory, chipmaking equipment, networking and optics, servers, and power and cooling. I left out the four AI-related names that are already in the BBP Portfolio.
Then I ran four filters, one after the other:
1. Revenue up at least 50% in the last reported quarter, year over year.
24 companies passed.
2. Positive free cash flow over the last 12 months.
Growth that burns cash doesn't count. 20 passed.
3. More cash than debt.
If the cycle turns, nobody gets forced to sell or borrow. 13 passed.
4. At least 40% below the 52-week high.
The point is to find what got cheap, not what kept running. 9 passed.
A few of the names that didn't make it are worth noticing.
Nvidia passed every filter except the last one. It's only 29% below its high.
Super Micro is growing almost 300%, and it still burns cash.
Dell and Amphenol are growing fast, but they carry more debt than cash.
THE 9 SURVIVORS
Nine companies that are still growing at least 50%, generating cash and holding more cash than debt. And every one of them trades at least 48% below its high.
Memory makers, chip equipment, servers, power, optics. The selloff didn't spare anyone.
I only bought one.
1 I BOUGHT: CREDO
Credo makes the connections inside AI data centers.

Thousands of GPUs only work as one machine if they can move data between each other fast enough. Credo sells the cables and chips that do it: active electrical cables, copper cables with a chip at each end that cleans the signal, plus optical chips and the components that keep the signal strong over longer distances.
It works with five hyperscalers, the companies that run the largest cloud data centers.
The business kept growing straight through the crash.
Revenue in the quarter to August 1: 479 million dollars, up 115% year over year.
Guidance for the current quarter: 525 to 535 million dollars.
Full-year guidance: revenue up more than 85%, with an adjusted net margin of around 50%.
Free cash flow over the last 12 months: 439 million dollars.
Cash and short-term investments: 764 million dollars, against 21 million of debt.
The stock did something very different.
It went from 87.81 dollars in March to 302.52 dollars in June. Then it gave almost all of it back: 112.33 dollars at the close on November 5. Down 63% from the top.
Three things pushed it down:
The results on September 1 beat expectations, but GAAP margins fell and costs jumped. The stock dropped 20% the next day.

On November 2, Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal worth 115 billion dollars, a bet that optical links will replace copper inside data centers. Credo's biggest product is a copper cable.
After the November 3 midterms, investors started pricing in limits on new data centers. Credo fell 32% in a week. The company didn't report any bad news of its own.
That gap, between what the business did and what the stock did, is why I bought.
But there is a real risk, and it's not a small one.
Four customers made up 84% of last quarter's revenue. The biggest alone was 33%. If one of them slows orders, the numbers change fast.
Below: why I picked Credo over the other 8 survivors, what I think it's worth in three scenarios, the price I'd add more at, what would make me sell, and whether it goes into the BBP Portfolio.
WHY CREDO AND NOT THE OTHER 8
On price alone, Credo isn't the cheapest survivor. These are the reasons I passed on the others:

SanDisk and Western Digital trade at 3x and 7x next year's expected earnings. They are the cheapest, but memory and storage earnings move with prices, and prices move in cycles. Cheap earnings at the top of a cycle can turn expensive very quickly.
Lumentum is being bought by Marvell in an all-stock deal. Buying Lumentum today mostly means buying Marvell.
Celestica grows fast, but it assembles servers. Its operating margin was 7.9% last quarter. Credo's was 25.2% (GAAP) and 48.2% adjusted.
Astera Labs is the closest business to Credo: connectivity chips inside AI servers, growing 154%. It trades at 30x next year's earnings. Credo trades at 13x.
Vertiv, Lam Research and Teradyne are great companies growing 54% to 70%, at 18x to 21x next year's earnings. Credo grows faster for less.
Credo is the one where growth, margins and price line up best for me.
WHAT IT COULD BE WORTH

Analysts expect adjusted earnings per share of 6.31 dollars this fiscal year, which ends in April 2027, and 9.71 dollars next year. At Tuesday's close of 129.80 dollars, that's 20.6x this year and 13.4x next year.
For reference, its average forward P/E over the last three years was c. 63x, according to Yahoo Finance.
Bear, 105 dollars (-19%):
growth stalls because a top customer cuts orders or switches to a rival. Earnings of 7 dollars at 15x.
Base, 194 dollars (+49%):
the consensus of 9.71 dollars at 20x. Still far below its three-year average multiple.
Bull, 288 dollars (+122%):
optics ramps faster than expected and the multiple recovers part of the way. 11.50 dollars at 25x. That's still below the June high.
These are my scenarios, not forecasts.
Where I'd add more:
below 120 dollars. Above 194 dollars, the base case is priced in and I'd stop buying.
WHAT WOULD MAKE ME SELL
Revenue for the quarter to October comes in below 525 million dollars, the bottom of the guidance, or the full-year growth target of 85% gets cut.
One of the top two customers drops below 20% of revenue without new customers making up for it.
The adjusted gross margin falls below 67%, the bottom of the current guidance.
One more thing to watch:
stock-based pay jumped to 88 million dollars last quarter, from 50 million the quarter before. That cost is real even if adjusted earnings leave it out.
Next test:
results in early December. The date isn't announced yet.
THE BBP PORTFOLIO

Credo stays on the BBP Portfolio radar, not in the portfolio. The portfolio already holds three AI chip suppliers, and I want to see the December results before adding a fourth. If the quarter confirms the guidance, it goes in, and you'll see it in the app first.
HOW I'D USE THIS LIST
The 9 survivors are a starting point, not a shopping list. Each one passed four simple filters on numbers that are already public. None of that says what happens next quarter.

If you own AI suppliers already, this list shows which ones the market is selling for reasons that have little to do with their own results. If you don't, it's a list worth watching before the next round of earnings.

Data as of the November 10, 2026 close. Sources: company filings and results releases, Credo's Q1 fiscal 2027 earnings call, Shibui Finance, StockAnalysis consensus estimates. Growth is the last reported quarter, year over year. Next fiscal year differs by company.
Disclosure:
I own shares of Credo in my personal account.
Not financial advice. Do your own research before investing.
